t: How To Eliminate The Gray Area From Your Class Rules
q: The gray area occurs when you witness behavior you don’t like. —But are uncertain whether or not it breaks a class rule.
The short answer is that you must eliminate them. Because if you don’t, the problems will expand and worsen as time goes on.
My answer: “Do you want your students to be able to do that?
It’s not how restrictive you are that determines how well behaved your class is. It’s setting your boundaries as you prefer, teaching them explicitly to your students, and then holding to them.
The good news is that they’re mere slivers of uncertainty, not giant swaths.
For them, being aware of the existence of these cloudy bars of incertitude, and getting rid of them, has been a revelation.
This is a big problem because unless you’re aware of your weaknesses, you can’t address them. You’ll continue to struggle and not know why.
If you’re uncertain about what does and doesn’t constitute transgressing your rules, then you’ll waffle when it comes to enforcing them.
In fact, trying to convince students to behave only reinforces the image they have of you as weak and easily manipulated.
You’ll have to raise your voice and repeat yourself just to be heard. Just getting through lessons becomes an exercise in frustration.
Being viewed by students as a pushover doesn’t mean that you’re not a strong person. Just deciding to become a teacher and showing up every day is proof that you are strong.
Commit to it mind, body, and soul and the perception of you as a pushover will be gone in a week.
